archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergrad research since the end of my sophomore year. It's been an eye-opening experience that has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but it turned out to be a great decision.
archival_memory.research_lab_description: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work together to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In contrast to the small data projects we often do in classes, our lab deals with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. My main task is to create front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
archival_memory.first_research_project: My first research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific, resulting in a massive amount of raw data. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designed interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. The project culminated in co-authoring my first paper on the system. Seeing my name in an official publication was a surreal experience, and it remains one of my proudest moments in college.
archival_memory.current_research_focus: My current research focus is on immersive analytics platforms, specifically exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' intuitive understanding of complex data. By providing a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, scientists can interact with it in a more immersive way, such as walking around, touching, and highlighting subsets. This approach offers a significant leap beyond traditional 2D visuals and numerical data in spreadsheets. The process involves experimentation with VR headsets, integration with engines like Unity or Unreal, and optimizing data streaming into the 3D environment. It's a cutting-edge field, and I'm excited to be at the forefront of it, forging my own path as there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
archival_memory.research_life: Research life is often misunderstood as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away on a mysterious project. However, it's actually a lot of reading. Academic papers never end, and when I'm trying to solve a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has tried something similar and written about it in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through those papers to find relevant information. It can be overwhelming, but over time, I've learned how to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I discover something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I have the opportunity to interact with a diverse group of graduate students, both master's and PhD candidates. Initially, it can be intimidating to engage with individuals who are deeply immersed in their niche fields. However, it's also incredibly inspiring to be surrounded by such expertise and passion. One PhD student in our lab is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets, with the goal of integrating it with our VR platform. This innovative approach would allow us to display a compressed representation of the data in VR, reducing the need to load every single point at once. It's a practical solution for enhancing real-time performance. Working alongside this student provides me with a unique perspective on how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-world scenarios. Some of our most productive brainstorming sessions occur spontaneously, often during casual conversations in the lab break room or over coffee. These interactions allow us to explore creative solutions, such as offloading processing tasks to the GPU. It's a truly collaborative and dynamic environment.
archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present our research through poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience that required me to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, imagining that professors or industry professionals might ask tough questions. However, the reality was quite different. The atmosphere was more like a friendly dialogue, with people genuinely interested in what we're doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It was eye-opening to see how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
archival_memory.publications: I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission. The conference we're targeting is the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS), which is a significant event in our field. Our research focuses on a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. We hypothesize that VR immersion enables researchers to identify anomalies or trends more quickly than with 2D charts. To test this, we conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recording their times and gathering UX feedback. Now, we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with different team members handling specific sections. I'm responsible for the system architecture and prototype design, while others are working on the user study methodology and our PI is weaving everything together. It's a delicate balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project on the side.
archival_memory.future_plans: I'm often asked if I plan on pursuing a graduate degree. Currently, I'm considering working in the industry for a couple of years, ideally at a tech company that values R&D and advanced solution building. This will give me a chance to see how cutting-edge concepts like data visualization and machine learning are applied in real product development. My mentor in the lab suggested that industry experience can provide a valuable perspective on what problems are truly relevant, which would be beneficial if I decide to return for a PhD with a more practical approach. I'm excited about the prospect of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge, but I also want to gain hands-on experience before making a decision.
archival_memory.frustrations_in_research: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your entire idea has already been done and improved upon by a group in Europe or elsewhere. It can be disheartening, but the key is to adapt. By reading the existing paper, incorporating their findings, and finding a new angle or application, you can push the boundaries of your research. This is the essence of research – building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special. It's a reminder that we're never starting from scratch, but rather, we're standing on the shoulders of giants.
archival_memory.server_crash_story: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, taking vital data with it. Some of the data wasn't fully backed up, which was a rookie mistake on our part. The night of the crash was chaotic, with frantic email chains and Zoom calls with the lab manager as everyone scrambled to see if we could recover the data. Fortunately, we were able to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of having a reliable backup system in place. In response, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we wouldn't rely on a single point of failure again. It was a stressful experience, but it also brought the lab together and taught us a valuable lesson.
archival_memory.connection_with_professors: Research has allowed me to connect with professors on a more personal level, beyond just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is incredibly approachable, and I can easily pop into her office to discuss anything from career direction to struggles in class. She's been a great mentor, recommending me for various scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. One such opportunity was a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, where I had the chance to engage with academic experts from around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even engage in light-hearted banter over rival theories was truly fascinating. It felt like I was experiencing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time. These connections have been invaluable in my research journey.
archival_memory.research_journey: My journey in the research world has been a wild ride so far. It's been a lot of hard work, often chaotic, but also incredibly rewarding. I love the feeling that the work we do in the lab could potentially shape the way scientists understand their data in five or ten years. The idea that the VR and immersive technologies we're pioneering might become standard tools in the future is a thrilling prospect. I'm motivated by the sense of contributing to something bigger and leaving a lasting impact. Whether or not I decide to pursue a graduate degree soon, this experience has profoundly changed my perspective on computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergraduate years without it – it's enriched my entire understanding of what it means to be a computer scientist.
archival_memory.student_vibrant_campus_life: Yeah, campus life here is pretty vibrant—there’s just so much going on, sometimes it’s tough to keep track of everything. As a fourth-year Computer Science student, I’ve definitely seen how the culture has evolved over the years, and I’ve discovered a bunch of different communities that make this place feel like a second home. You’d be surprised how many ways there are to get involved beyond just coding in front of your laptop all day.
archival_memory.student_vibrant_campus_life_short: Campus life is vibrant with many ways to get involved beyond coding.
archival_memory.student_clubs: One of my biggest regrets was not joining more clubs during my freshman year. I was overwhelmed by the transition from high school to college and focused on my classes. However, I eventually realized that the campus experience is about more than just academics. I joined a couple of student organizations, including the Computer Science Society. They host weekly meetups where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and sometimes have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment, even for beginners. If I'm stuck on a tricky concept or need insight into topics like concurrency or containerization, I can chat with fellow members who have worked on similar projects in their internships.
archival_memory.student_clubs_short: I regret not joining more clubs during my freshman year. I was overwhelmed by the transition and focused on classes. However, I eventually realized that the campus experience is about more than academics. I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups to discuss new technologies, share projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. If I'm stuck on a concept or need insight, I can chat with members who have worked on similar projects in their internships.
archival_memory.student_vr_ar_club: I've been attending the VR/AR Club on and off since my sophomore year. I got hooked when I started researching immersive analytics, so it was natural to want to hang out with people who share that passion. The club is surprisingly hands-on, with a VR lab in the engineering building equipped with headsets, sensors, and quirky prototypes built by past members. We host demos where each person showcases their latest project, whether it's a mini-game or something more experimental like augmented reality interfaces for everyday tasks. A few weeks ago, someone showcased an AR tutor concept for advanced math, where you could point your phone at an equation on your paper and get a hint or a 3D demonstration. The creativity inspires me to push my own research further. I love the supportive vibe when people are genuinely excited about emerging tech.
archival_memory.student_radio_station: The campus is also big on non-tech stuff. I'm not super involved, but I do pop into the student-run radio station events now and then. They host open-mic nights that are a blast – people sing, read poetry, or perform stand-up comedy. I remember one night, a friend from my Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. He's usually so quiet in class, but on stage, he was belting out soulful tunes as if he was born for it. Moments like that remind me there's always more to someone than meets the eye when you're just coding together or doing group projects.
archival_memory.student_central_lawn: The campus has these iconic spots, like the huge central lawn where students often hang out between classes. It's common for student organizations to set up booths there, promoting their clubs and handing out freebies like stickers or candy to attract new members. My personal weakness is free pizza, so if a club includes that in their advertisement, I'm easily tempted. The lawn is also where some of the biggest campus events take place, such as our annual Tech Fest. During Tech Fest, project teams showcase their prototypes, and recruiters often attend, looking for innovative ideas. It's a big deal here, especially for engineering and CS students.
archival_memory.student_campus_culture: I'd say campus culture is fairly collaborative. There are pockets of competition, especially among seniors trying to land top internships or job offers, but overall, people want to help each other succeed. I remember the campus hackathon in my second year, which was a huge eye-opener. Thousands of students from various backgrounds, from first-years to master's candidates, crammed into the student center for 24 or 36 hours straight, hacking away. It was chaotic but exhilarating. You'd see beginners learning the basics of GitHub while advanced teams used complex machine learning libraries to do real-time image recognition. Sponsors and mentors wandered around to see if anyone needed help. I formed a small team with a few casual acquaintances, and the bond we formed during that all-nighter – eating stale pizza at 3 a.m., debugging code, and deliriously cheering each other on – was unlike anything I'd experienced before. That's the vibe I associate with campus life: you're all in the trenches together, forging friendships through shared experiences and challenges.
archival_memory.student_dorm_life: Dorm life can be a huge part of campus culture. In my first two years, I stayed in a dorm specifically for engineering majors, which we jokingly called "The Engi-House." Late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary. Someone would be frantically working on an assignment for Data Structures, while another group might be streaming e-sports tournaments. Occasionally, the environment got a bit too intense, with stressed-out engineers fueled by energy drinks. However, it also meant that if you encountered a stumbling block, there was always someone nearby who could offer a quick pointer. Beyond academics, we'd hold potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a small talent show to blow off steam.
archival_memory.student_volunteering: Volunteering at outreach events has been a big part of my campus life. The CS department organizes a "Tech for Good" day where local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. Volunteers like me help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's incredibly rewarding to see younger students light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage. I remember how I felt at that age – like the tech world was so vast and intimidating. Giving them a positive first experience is something I take pride in. Events like these show a different side of campus, beyond academic research and class assignments. It's about engaging with the community and inspiring the next generation to get excited about STEM fields.
archival_memory.student_social_scene: The social scene on campus is pretty lively, offering a break from academic life. Greek life is present for those interested, but I personally didn't join a fraternity. Instead, I found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people who share your interests. For example, a friend who's super into robotics joined the Robotics Team in his first semester and found a second family there. They now hang out on weekends, watch movies together, and grab dinner. Similarly, I've grown close to folks in the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk shop when we're together; we also joke around, complain about cafeteria food, or plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails.
archival_memory.student_senior_week: Senior Week is a staple of campus culture. It's a series of events leading up to graduation, including a formal dance, a carnival, and a day where seniors get their photos taken in caps and gowns at iconic campus landmarks. I've heard it's bittersweet – it's the last hurrah before everyone scatters. My older friends who graduated last year said it was one of the best weeks of their college life, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a bit of that sinking feeling that the journey's almost over. I'm both excited and a little anxious for it. I've been here for four years, made so many memories, and it's weird to think about not being a student anymore.
archival_memory.student_rivalry_game: The Rivalry Game is a big campus tradition. Our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college in various sports. Although I'm not a die-hard sports fan, I love the energy on campus during that week. People show their school spirit by wearing colors, painting their faces, and carrying banners. Sometimes, the night before the big football game, we have a massive pep rally with fireworks. It's a spectacle that's hard to miss. Even if you don't attend the game itself, the campus vibe is electric. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer together. Whether we win or lose, the celebrations or commiserations can last all weekend. It's a unifying moment for everyone, from business majors to art students to us nerdy engineers.
archival_memory.student_e_sports: The e-sports team has gained official recognition on campus. It's great to see a broader definition of competition and community. During tournaments, you can find a wide seating area and a big screen streaming the matches live. It's not uncommon for a hundred or more students to gather and cheer on our team for League of Legends or Overwatch matches. I never would've guessed e-sports would be a legitimate campus institution when I started college, but times are changing. It's awesome to see the evolution of the campus sports scene.
archival_memory.student_midnight_breakfast: The Midnight Breakfast during finals week is a beloved tradition. It's a time when stressed-out students come together for pancakes and cereal at midnight. Professors join in to serve food, the school band might perform, and everyone takes a collective break from studying. It's a small gesture, but it goes a long way in reminding us that we're not alone in feeling anxious about final exams. It's traditions like these that make me appreciate the campus culture – there's a genuine effort to ensure students have some fun and camaraderie even during high-pressure times.
archival_memory.student_campus_life: Campus life is what you make of it. If you're willing to explore, approach new people, and join clubs, you'll find a million ways to enrich your experience. It's easy to get lost in your workload, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science, but I've found that attending events, volunteering, and connecting with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. When I look back on my four years, I'll remember the late-night coding, sure, but also the silly game nights in the dorm, the Tech Fest presentations, the hackathon adrenaline, and the excited cheers at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. If you ever want a quick tour, I'd be happy to show you some of my favorite spots and introduce you to a few clubs. There's something for everyone here, and I'm so glad I finally embraced all the campus has to offer.
